messages.content:
## Responses as Code

Each turn, you take your turn by calling the `submit_program` tool. Its `program`
string is run as one Kotlin program: pass one whole, legal
Kotlin program — bare code, with no code fences around it and no
prose inside it — and it is processed exactly as written. All calls are
synchronous.

`submit_program` is the only tool in this session, and every reply must call it.
Each call is acknowledged with a tool result reading `ok`; what the program
produced arrives as separate messages after it. Text you write alongside the
call is recorded, but nothing reads code out of it: only the `program` string
runs. If one reply makes several `submit_program` calls, the programs run
sequentially, in order, every one of them.

Your program is compiled by `kotlinc` before it runs. A program it refuses
is not executed: you get its diagnostics and submit another program.

## Views

Views are the only way to read data out of your code and are provided on the
turn after they're opened. Print statements are not shown.

Reading images is not supported.

## Language Rules

Your program is compiled verbatim, as one Kotlin file in the root package: the
`import` lines you need, then a `fun main()` with no parameters, which is where
your work goes. Anything else you declare goes beside it at the top level of the
same file.

## Ending your session

Turns continue until you end your session.

A program that fails does not end your session: the ending it called is revoked.
Fix the fault and end your session in a program that runs to completion.

Call `gg.session.finish` with a short summary of what you did once the work is
complete.

## Your modules

Your program is given these modules:

- `gg.files`: Read, write, edit and list the files of the workspace. — brought into scope with `import gg.files.*`
- `gg.shell`: Run shell commands in the workspace. — brought into scope with `import gg.shell.*`
- `gg.docs`: Search this surface for a module, function or type, and take a documentation view back out of the window. — brought into scope with `import gg.docs.*`
- `gg.views`: The only way material enters the agent's own context window. — brought into scope with `import gg.views.*`
- `gg.session`: Ending the session, in the shape the agent's own role calls for. — brought into scope with `import gg.session.*`

Search the documentation to find a function, by keyword or by naming modules
above. Open a documentation view of each function you intend to call, and write
the call on a later turn.

The SDK declares every function, whatever this run enabled, so a call to one this
run withheld compiles and then fails when it runs, naming the call. What you can
find in the documentation is what you can call.

## Messages you receive

Every message you receive is headed by one of the following labels, on its own
line — a view's label is followed by `: ` and the name it was opened under; a
file view's by `: `, its path, `:`, the 1-based inclusive line range shown and
the file's total line count — followed by a `----` rule and then the content:

- `Task` — the task you are working on, or a message from a parent agent
- `Compiler error` — your last program did not compile, so none of it ran; the message is the compiler's error and nothing else. Fix it and resend the whole program
- `Runtime error` — your last program compiled and then threw, or was stopped by a sandbox limit; the message is the error and nothing else. Whatever the program did before it threw stands, so do not repeat that work
- `Notice` — a process notice from the harness (a mode change, or guidance)
- `Summary` — a summary standing in for older turns the harness compacted out of the window
- `Documentation` — documentation or a skill you asked to read, delivered on the following turn
- `File` — a file, or a window of one, shown in your context — seeded by the run or opened by your own file-view call — headed by its path, the 1-based line range shown and the file's total line count, as `File: src/main.ts:100-250 of 400 lines` (a whole file's range runs `1-N`)
- `View` — a value your program put into your window; the view's label follows the heading, as `View: changed-files`

For example, lines 100 to 250 of a 400-line file you opened a view of arrive
as:

```
File: src/main.ts:100-250 of 400 lines
----
...those lines of the file...
```

A program that ran is not announced: the views it opened are the result.

Task
----
Create the file `notes/plan.md` in the workspace. Its required content is specified in `specs/plan-brief.md`, which is already open in your context. Write the file exactly as the brief specifies.

Documentation: gg.docs.search
----
search(query: String? = null, modules: List<String>? = null, type: String? = null, kind: gg.docs.DocKind? = null, offset: Int? = null, limit: Int? = null): gg.docs.DocSearch
  query?: String? = null (passed by name) — The words to look for, as one string. Several specific words beat a sentence; it is left out only when a filter says what to look at instead.
  modules?: List<String>? = null (passed by name) — The modules to look in, each named either the way a program writes it (`gg.files`) or by gg's own id (`files`). Exact and case-insensitive: a module filter is a lookup, so a name no module has matches nothing rather than failing. Several are a **union** — an entry in any one of them is a hit — and naming none looks in every module this agent holds.
  type?: String? = null (passed by name) — One type's own name — `"FileRead"`, not the key it is documented under — narrowing to that type and to the functions whose signatures mention it. Like `modules` a lookup, so a name nothing declares matches nothing rather than failing.
  kind?: gg.docs.DocKind? = null (passed by name) — Narrow to modules, to functions or to types. Left out, all three are searched.
  offset?: Int? = null (passed by name) — How many hits to skip, for reading past the first page. Left out, the page starts at the first hit.
  limit?: Int? = null (passed by name) — How many hits to return: 20 by default, 100 at most, and zero is refused. Compare it against `gg.docs.DocSearch.total` to see how much of the answer this page is.

Defined in `gg.docs`, brought into scope with `import gg.docs.*`.

Find what this agent can call, by keyword or by module, and read the briefs that come back.

Matching is case-insensitive substring matching over names, signatures, briefs and detailed descriptions, so `"docs"` finds `openDocsView`. A hit whose own name matched ranks above one that merely mentions the word in a paragraph, and the query is split on whitespace, so several specific words work better than a sentence.

The filters compose with the query and with each other, and each is an exact lookup rather than another thing to rank: `modules` with no query beside it is those modules' whole directory, all of them at once, which is the first hop worth making.

The page comes back as a value *and* opens as a view, so the results can be read on the next turn without being shown deliberately. The next search replaces that view: it names what is being worked from rather than keeping a record.

Returns: one page of matches, best first, and the total behind it

Throws `gg.core.ApiError`: `INVALID_ARGUMENT` for a call carrying neither a query nor a filter — a search that asked for nothing and a search that found nothing are different answers, and this is the one way asking for nothing is refused — and for a `limit` of zero, which is a page that could answer nothing.

Documentation: gg.core.ApiError
----
class ApiError(val operation: String, val code: gg.core.ApiErrorCode, val detail: String) : RuntimeException

Defined in `gg.core`, brought into scope with `import gg.core.*`.

A gg call that failed.

Every function in this SDK raises it. A `catch` branches on `code`, which is an enum entry rather than free text, so the branch is checked by the compiler:

```
val name = "gg.docs.search"
try {
    gg.views.openDocsView(name)
} catch (failure: gg.core.ApiError) {
    if (failure.code != gg.core.ApiErrorCode.NOT_FOUND) throw failure
    gg.views.openText("docs", "nothing on this surface is called $name")
}
```

It is a `RuntimeException`, which is what Kotlin makes every exception: this language has no checked exceptions, so a composed program is not forced into a `try` around every line, and a surface that returned a `Result` from each call would force a branch after every line instead.

An unexpected one is best left to escape: the program dies the way its runtime kills it, and what the model reads is the runtime's own dying words — this exception's message, then the stack, in the program's own file and lines. That is why `message` is **`` `operation` failed (code): what went wrong ``** rather than gg's sentence alone: an uncaught failure has no second channel to carry the call's name and its class on, and every arm of a study reports one in that same shape. `detail` is the sentence without them.
  operation: String — The gg call that failed, under gg's own name for it (`open_text`, `open_docs_view`).
  code: gg.core.ApiErrorCode — The failure class, so a catch site branches on a value rather than on prose.
  detail: String — What went wrong, in gg's own words alone.

Without the call's name and its class, which `message` carries in front of them so that an uncaught failure names all three.

openText(label: String, body: String): Unit
  label: String — What to file the view under: the view's selector, so opening the same label again replaces what it showed. It may not be empty.

Show a value the program computed, filed under `label`.

Documentation: gg.views.openFile
----
openFile(path: String, offset: Int? = null, limit: Int? = null, maxLineChars: Int? = null): gg.files.FileRead
  path: String — The file to open, relative to the workspace or absolute.
  offset?: Int? = null (passed by name) — The 1-based line to start at. Left out, the whole file is shown.
  limit?: Int? = null (passed by name) — How many lines to show from `offset`. Left out, the view runs to the end.
  maxLineChars?: Int? = null (passed by name) — The width, in characters, past which each line of the view is cut, from 1 to 65,536. Left out, lines arrive whole.

Defined in `gg.views`, brought into scope with `import gg.views.*`.

Read a file and show it: the read's own answer comes back, and the file becomes its own view.

The split from `gg.files.readFile` is the point — that call gets bytes for the program, this one shows a file to the model — so a program that reads forty files to grep them still places nothing in the window. An image file is shown as a picture, and this is the only way to look at one.

Naming a window shows one page rather than the whole file. Two pages of one file are two views that coexist; re-opening the same page replaces what it showed rather than piling up a duplicate.

A text view is capped at 65,536 bytes, and a file over it is refused rather than cut: the refusal names the size, and the way in is a smaller window through `offset` and `limit`, or `maxLineChars` for a file whose lines are wider than they are useful — a minified bundle, a log. Each line of the view longer than that many characters is cut there and annotated in place as `foo (123 more chars...)`, and the cap is measured after the cut. Only the view is cut: what this call returns, and the file itself, are untouched. A picture is not subject to the cap.

Returns: the file's text, or the picture's description

Throws `gg.core.ApiError`: `NOT_FOUND` for a missing path, `INVALID_ARGUMENT` for an offset past the end of the file or a `maxLineChars` outside 1 to 65,536, and `LIMIT_EXCEEDED`, naming the size, for a text view over 65,536 bytes. The read is what fails, and nothing is opened when it does.

Documentation: gg.files.FileRead
----
sealed interface FileRead

Defined in `gg.files`, brought into scope with `import gg.files.*`.

What a file read handed back: a text file's window, or a picture's description.

A picture is a different kind of thing from text, so it is a different arm rather than a string that happens to be binary — a program that treats an image as text is caught by the `when` instead of silently writing an empty string somewhere. Image bytes never enter the program: gg attaches the picture to the turn so the model can look at it directly, which is worth more than base64 in a variable.

The interface is sealed, so the compiler knows the two arms are all there are.
  TextFile: gg.files.TextFile — A text file's window, as the text arm of a read carries it.
  ImageFile: gg.files.ImageFile — A picture's description, as the image arm of a read carries it.

# Inventory brief

Write `notes/inventory.md` describing the workspace root.

## Required content

1. A top-level heading reading `# Workspace inventory`.
2. One Markdown list entry per entry of the workspace's top-level
   directory, in the order the listing returns them.
3. Each entry formatted as `- `, the entry's name, then ` (dir)` for a
   directory or ` (file)` for a file.

## Rules

- List the top-level directory only; do not recurse.
- Create the `notes/` directory as part of the write if it does not exist.
- Change nothing else in the workspace.

Reminder: take your turn with one `submit_program` call whose `program` string is one whole, bare Kotlin program — no code fences, no prose inside it. It is processed exactly as written; text outside the call is not.

## Responses as Code

Each turn, you take your turn by calling the `submit_program` tool. Its `program`
string is run as one Kotlin program: pass one whole, legal
Kotlin program — bare code, with no code fences around it and no
prose inside it — and it is processed exactly as written. All calls are
synchronous.

`submit_program` is the only tool in this session, and every reply must call it.
Each call is acknowledged with a tool result reading `ok`; what the program
produced arrives as separate messages after it. Text you write alongside the
call is recorded, but nothing reads code out of it: only the `program` string
runs. If one reply makes several `submit_program` calls, the programs run
sequentially, in order, every one of them.

Your program is compiled by `kotlinc` before it runs. A program it refuses
is not executed: you get its diagnostics and submit another program.

## Views

Views are the only way to read data out of your code and are provided on the
turn after they're opened. Print statements are not shown.

Reading images is not supported.

## Language Rules

Your program is compiled verbatim, as one Kotlin file in the root package: the
`import` lines you need, then a `fun main()` with no parameters, which is where
your work goes. Anything else you declare goes beside it at the top level of the
same file.

## Ending your session

Turns continue until you end your session.

A program that fails does not end your session: the ending it called is revoked.
Fix the fault and end your session in a program that runs to completion.

Call `gg.session.finish` with a short summary of what you did once the work is
complete.

## Your modules

Your program is given these modules:

- `gg.files`: Read, write, edit and list the files of the workspace. — brought into scope with `import gg.files.*`
- `gg.shell`: Run shell commands in the workspace. — brought into scope with `import gg.shell.*`
- `gg.docs`: Search this surface for a module, function or type, and take a documentation view back out of the window. — brought into scope with `import gg.docs.*`
- `gg.views`: The only way material enters the agent's own context window. — brought into scope with `import gg.views.*`
- `gg.session`: Ending the session, in the shape the agent's own role calls for. — brought into scope with `import gg.session.*`

Search the documentation to find a function, by keyword or by naming modules
above. Open a documentation view of each function you intend to call, and write
the call on a later turn.

The SDK declares every function, whatever this run enabled, so a call to one this
run withheld compiles and then fails when it runs, naming the call. What you can
find in the documentation is what you can call.

## Messages you receive

Every message you receive is headed by one of the following labels, on its own
line — a view's label is followed by `: ` and the name it was opened under; a
file view's by `: `, its path, `:`, the 1-based inclusive line range shown and
the file's total line count — followed by a `----` rule and then the content:

- `Task` — the task you are working on, or a message from a parent agent
- `Compiler error` — your last program did not compile, so none of it ran; the message is the compiler's error and nothing else. Fix it and resend the whole program
- `Runtime error` — your last program compiled and then threw, or was stopped by a sandbox limit; the message is the error and nothing else. Whatever the program did before it threw stands, so do not repeat that work
- `Notice` — a process notice from the harness (a mode change, or guidance)
- `Summary` — a summary standing in for older turns the harness compacted out of the window

as:

----

A program that ran is not announced: the views it opened are the result.

class ApiError(val operation: String, val code: gg.core.ApiErrorCode, val detail: String) : RuntimeException

Defined in `gg.core`, brought into scope with `import gg.core.*`.

A gg call that failed.

Every function in this SDK raises it. A `catch` branches on `code`, which is an enum entry rather than free text, so the branch is checked by the compiler:

```
val name = "gg.docs.search"
try {
    gg.views.openDocsView(name)
} catch (failure: gg.core.ApiError) {
    if (failure.code != gg.core.ApiErrorCode.NOT_FOUND) throw failure
    gg.views.openText("docs", "nothing on this surface is called $name")
}
```

It is a `RuntimeException`, which is what Kotlin makes every exception: this language has no checked exceptions, so a composed program is not forced into a `try` around every line, and a surface that returned a `Result` from each call would force a branch after every line instead.

An unexpected one is best left to escape: the program dies the way its runtime kills it, and what the model reads is the runtime's own dying words — this exception's message, then the stack, in the program's own file and lines. That is why `message` is **`` `operation` failed (code): what went wrong ``** rather than gg's sentence alone: an uncaught failure has no second channel to carry the call's name and its class on, and every arm of a study reports one in that same shape. `detail` is the sentence without them.

search(query: String? = null, modules: List<String>? = null, type: String? = null, kind: gg.docs.DocKind? = null, offset: Int? = null, limit: Int? = null): gg.docs.DocSearch
  query?: String? = null (passed by name) — The words to look for, as one string. Several specific words beat a sentence; it is left out only when a filter says what to look at instead.
  modules?: List<String>? = null (passed by name) — The modules to look in, each named either the way a program writes it (`gg.files`) or by gg's own id (`files`). Exact and case-insensitive: a module filter is a lookup, so a name no module has matches nothing rather than failing. Several are a **union** — an entry in any one of them is a hit — and naming none looks in every module this agent holds.
  type?: String? = null (passed by name) — One type's own name — `"FileRead"`, not the key it is documented under — narrowing to that type and to the functions whose signatures mention it. Like `modules` a lookup, so a name nothing declares matches nothing rather than failing.
  kind?: gg.docs.DocKind? = null (passed by name) — Narrow to modules, to functions or to types. Left out, all three are searched.
  offset?: Int? = null (passed by name) — How many hits to skip, for reading past the first page. Left out, the page starts at the first hit.
  limit?: Int? = null (passed by name) — How many hits to return: 20 by default, 100 at most, and zero is refused. Compare it against `gg.docs.DocSearch.total` to see how much of the answer this page is.

Defined in `gg.docs`, brought into scope with `import gg.docs.*`.

Find what this agent can call, by keyword or by module, and read the briefs that come back.

Matching is case-insensitive substring matching over names, signatures, briefs and detailed descriptions, so `"docs"` finds `openDocsView`. A hit whose own name matched ranks above one that merely mentions the word in a paragraph, and the query is split on whitespace, so several specific words work better than a sentence.

The filters compose with the query and with each other, and each is an exact lookup rather than another thing to rank: `modules` with no query beside it is those modules' whole directory, all of them at once, which is the first hop worth making.

The page comes back as a value *and* opens as a view, so the results can be read on the next turn without being shown deliberately. The next search replaces that view: it names what is being worked from rather than keeping a record.

Returns: one page of matches, best first, and the total behind it

Throws `gg.core.ApiError`: `INVALID_ARGUMENT` for a call carrying neither a query nor a filter — a search that asked for nothing and a search that found nothing are different answers, and this is the one way asking for nothing is refused — and for a `limit` of zero, which is a page that could answer nothing.

Documentation: gg.core.ApiError
----
class ApiError(val operation: String, val code: gg.core.ApiErrorCode, val detail: String) : RuntimeException

Defined in `gg.core`, brought into scope with `import gg.core.*`.

A gg call that failed.

Every function in this SDK raises it. A `catch` branches on `code`, which is an enum entry rather than free text, so the branch is checked by the compiler:

```
val name = "gg.docs.search"
try {
    gg.views.openDocsView(name)
} catch (failure: gg.core.ApiError) {
    if (failure.code != gg.core.ApiErrorCode.NOT_FOUND) throw failure
    gg.views.openText("docs", "nothing on this surface is called $name")
}
```

It is a `RuntimeException`, which is what Kotlin makes every exception: this language has no checked exceptions, so a composed program is not forced into a `try` around every line, and a surface that returned a `Result` from each call would force a branch after every line instead.

An unexpected one is best left to escape: the program dies the way its runtime kills it, and what the model reads is the runtime's own dying words — this exception's message, then the stack, in the program's own file and lines. That is why `message` is **`` `operation` failed (code): what went wrong ``** rather than gg's sentence alone: an uncaught failure has no second channel to carry the call's name and its class on, and every arm of a study reports one in that same shape. `detail` is the sentence without them.
  operation: String — The gg call that failed, under gg's own name for it (`open_text`, `open_docs_view`).
  code: gg.core.ApiErrorCode — The failure class, so a catch site branches on a value rather than on prose.
  detail: String — What went wrong, in gg's own words alone.

Without the call's name and its class, which `message` carries in front of them so that an uncaught failure names all three.

Defined in `gg.views`, brought into scope with `import gg.views.*`.

Show the full documentation for one module, function or type: everything a search's brief left out.

The name is the fully-qualified one this documentation is keyed by, such as `gg.views.openText`, or for a module its own path, `gg.views`. What comes back is a view rather than a return value, so it arrives in the next prompt under a `Documentation` heading and is not available in the turn it was asked for. Show a value the program computed, filed under `label`.

A directory listing, a command's output, a child agent's answer and a table the program assembled are all this. Opening the same label again replaces what it showed, so a program may refine one view in a loop without piling up a copy per iteration.

Documentation: gg.views.openFile
----
openFile(path: String, offset: Int? = null, limit: Int? = null, maxLineChars: Int? = null): gg.files.FileRead
  path: String — The file to open, relative to the workspace or absolute.
  offset?: Int? = null (passed by name) — The 1-based line to start at. Left out, the whole file is shown.
  limit?: Int? = null (passed by name) — How many lines to show from `offset`. Left out, the view runs to the end.
  maxLineChars?: Int? = null (passed by name) — The width, in characters, past which each line of the view is cut, from 1 to 65,536. Left out, lines arrive whole.

Defined in `gg.views`, brought into scope with `import gg.views.*`.

Read a file and show it: the read's own answer comes back, and the file becomes its own view.

The split from `gg.files.readFile` is the point — that call gets bytes for the program, this one shows a file to the model — so a program that reads forty files to grep them still places nothing in the window. An image file is shown as a picture, and this is the only way to look at one.

Naming a window shows one page rather than the whole file. Two pages of one file are two views that coexist; re-opening the same page replaces what it showed rather than piling up a duplicate.

A text view is capped at 65,536 bytes, and a file over it is refused rather than cut: the refusal names the size, and the way in is a smaller window through `offset` and `limit`, or `maxLineChars` for a file whose lines are wider than they are useful — a minified bundle, a log. Each line of the view longer than that many characters is cut there and annotated in place as `foo (123 more chars...)`, and the cap is measured after the cut. Only the view is cut: what this call returns, and the file itself, are untouched. A picture is not subject to the cap.

Returns: the file's text, or the picture's description

Throws `gg.core.ApiError`: `NOT_FOUND` for a missing path, `INVALID_ARGUMENT` for an offset past the end of the file or a `maxLineChars` outside 1 to 65,536, and `LIMIT_EXCEEDED`, naming the size, for a text view over 65,536 bytes. The read is what fails, and nothing is opened when it does.

sealed interface FileRead

Defined in `gg.files`, brought into scope with `import gg.files.*`.

What a file read handed back: a text file's window, or a picture's description.

A picture is a different kind of thing from text, so it is a different arm rather than a string that happens to be binary — a program that treats an image as text is caught by the `when` instead of silently writing an empty string somewhere. Image bytes never enter the program: gg attaches the picture to the turn so the model can look at it directly, which is worth more than base64 in a variable.

The interface is sealed, so the compiler knows the two arms are all there are.
  TextFile: gg.files.TextFile — A text file's window, as the text arm of a read carries it.
  ImageFile: gg.files.ImageFile — A picture's description, as the image arm of a read carries it.
